title: GoCo: structure-guided conformal calibration for error-controlled Gene Ontology annotation release
comment: 34 pages, 5 figures, 15 tables; includes supplementary material
summary: Computational gene-function prediction generates annotations at a scale that experimental characterization cannot match, yet substantial errors remain even among leading methods. Explicit error-controlled calibration for Gene Ontology (GO) prediction remains largely undeveloped. We introduce GoCo, a structure-guided framework that calibrates how scores from an existing predictor are converted into released annotations. GoCo certifies a global threshold for a GO-hierarchy-aware gene-level false discovery proportion (FDP), then constructs a nested release path under the same asymptotic risk-control guarantee. At the primary operating point (alpha=0.10, delta=0.50), GoCo-M, developed on Wainberg co-essentiality modules and applied without retuning to three independent studies with the same shared-evidence structure, kept mean held-out gene-level FDP at or below target while releasing 6.3-17.6% more reference-supported GO terms than Multilabel. For gene-specific neighbourhoods, GoCo-N orders individual calls. Developed on FunMap and validated without retuning on the STRING v12.0 experiments-only network, GoCo-N released 33.8% and 36.4% more reference-supported GO terms than Multilabel on the same refined score grid in FunMap and STRING, respectively, while keeping mean held-out FDP below target. The same pattern held under the stricter delta=0.10 setting. Thus, predictor-native biological structure can be reused at calibration, not only prediction, to release more supported annotations at a chosen gene-level error target without retraining the predictor.

AI.tldr: GoCo is a structure-guided calibration framework that increases the number of reliable Gene Ontology annotations released by a predictor without retraining the model, while strictly controlling the gene-level false discovery proportion.
AI.motivation: Computational gene-function prediction scales well but suffers from high error rates, and existing methods lack explicit error-controlled calibration for Gene Ontology (GO) predictions.
AI.method: A structure-guided framework called GoCo that uses GO-hierarchy-aware calibration to certify global thresholds for gene-level false discovery proportion (FDP) and constructs nested release paths (GoCo-M and GoCo-N).
AI.result: GoCo-M and GoCo-N consistently maintained mean held-out FDP below target levels while increasing the release of reference-supported GO terms by 6.3-17.6% (GoCo-M) and 33.8-36.4% (GoCo-N) compared to Multilabel.
AI.conclusion: GoCo effectively uses predictor-native biological structure to calibrate scores into annotations, enabling the release of significantly more reference-supported GO terms while maintaining strict error control without retraining the original predictor.

title: TIAgent: From Natural Language to Grounded Agentic Workflows for Computational Pathology
summary: Computational pathology (CPath) analyses increasingly depend on multi-step computational workflows that require substantial programming expertise, limiting their accessibility to pathologists and other domain experts without extensive coding experience. Although large language models (LLMs) provide a promising natural-language interface for constructing such analyses, hallucinated operations and incorrect workflow specifications limit their reliability in scientific settings. We introduce Tissue Image Analysis Agent (TIAgent), an automated CPath workflow generation framework that, given a natural-language prompt specifying a complex analytical task together with an input dataset, automatically constructs a verifiable computational graph employing existing CPath operations. The resulting graph can be inspected and executed, enabling natural-language construction of complex CPath workflows for applications including automated biomarker discovery and tissue analysis. We demonstrate end-to-end workflow generation and execution and systematically benchmark 14 backbone LLMs across 90 unit tasks spanning 18 CPath operation types. The ability of each LLM to generate a complete and correct unit workflow is quantified using Unit Workflow Success (UWS). Performance varied substantially across backbone models, with Kimi-K2.7-Code achieving the highest UWS of 0.967 (95% CI: 0.907-0.989). Analysis of node and parameter correctness further revealed that selecting the appropriate computational operation and correctly configuring it represent distinct challenges for LLM-based workflow generation. TIAgent provides a foundation for making complex CPath workflow construction more accessible while enabling systematic evaluation of LLM-driven scientific workflow generation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces **TIAgent**, a framework designed to automate the generation of computational pathology (CPath) workflows using natural language, bridging the gap between complex programming requirements and domain experts like pathologists.
AI.motivation: Traditional CPath workflows require significant coding expertise. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a potential natural-language interface, they suffer from 'hallucinations' (incorrect operations or specifications), making them unreliable for scientific research.
AI.method: TIAgent converts natural-language prompts into **verifiable computational graphs** composed of existing CPath operations. This allows users to describe a task, have a workflow constructed, inspect it, and then execute it.
AI.result:
The researchers benchmarked 14 LLMs across 90 tasks. Key findings include:
  • **Kimi-K2.7-Code** was the top performer with a Unit Workflow Success (UWS) of **0.967**.
  • A distinction was identified between the difficulty of **selecting the correct operation** versus **configuring the correct parameters**.
AI.conclusion: TIAgent provides an accessible foundation for complex CPath analysis and establishes a systematic method for evaluating how LLMs perform in scientific workflow generation.

title: CausalOdyssey: Multi-Agent Local LLM Reasoning with Per-Patient Causal Structure for Rare Disease Retrieval
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Patients with rare diseases often wait years for a diagnosis. Existing HPO-based retrieval tools narrow the differential to a shortlist, but a clinician reading that shortlist has no signal for which candidate to trust or what to test next. We present CausalOdyssey, a local four-agent pipeline on Gemma 4 26B built over a classical IC-weighted gene-rescue backbone: a Diagnostician reranks the slate via chain-of-thought over per-patient FCI causal edges and Reactome mechanism context; a Verifier computes deterministic evidence against the top-1 (missing pathognomonic phenotypes, pathway chain closure) and has Gemma issue a confirm/flag/refute verdict over it; an Interrogator selects one follow-up HPO by split-variance scoring; a Narrator emits citation-validated clinical prose. Only the Diagnostician changes the ranking; the other three agents annotate it. On RareBench n=1,122, reranking a top-30 slate lifts R@1 by +12.57 pp over our structural baseline ([+10.07, +14.97]; p=8.3e-24). A no-LLM variant of that baseline, without its inverse disease-count weight, reaches a similar pooled R@1 (36.3% vs 35.3%): the LLM rerank is far better on metabolic cases (RAMEDIS, +16.0 pp) and far worse on case-report corpora (LIRICAL, MME), so its value is corpus-dependent. We also propose a masked-phenotype protocol for evaluating follow-up suggestions without an annotation-based oracle; under it, the Interrogator asks for a patient's hidden phenotypes no more often than simple baselines (0.6% vs 1.2%), although a perfect follow-up would add 11 pp at top-1. The Verifier's verdict separates correct from incorrect top-1s (51.4% vs 12.1% top-1 accuracy under confirm vs refute). For 30% of patients the gold diagnosis is outside our top-30, though LIRICAL retrieves over half of these. All inference is local; no patient data leaves the machine. Demo code and a live demo are public.

AI.tldr: CausalOdyssey is a local multi-agent LLM pipeline (using Gemma 4 26B) designed to improve rare disease diagnosis by reranking candidate diseases and providing clinical reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing HPO-based tools provide shortlists but lack actionable reasoning, confidence signals, or guidance on which phenotypes to test next.
AI.method: A four-agent local pipeline built on a classical IC-weighted gene-rescue backbone:
AI.result: Performance_Gain_R1_Plus_12.57pp_over_baseline_(p=8.3e-24)_(on_RareBench)_(noting_high_utility_in_metabolic_cases_but_lower_in_case_reports)_(Verifier_separates_correct_from_incorrect_top-1s_via_accuracy_disparity_51.4%_vs_12.1%)
AI.conclusion: The system enhances diagnostic accuracy and utility through reasoning and interrogation, though its effectiveness is highly dependent on the specific disease corpus used.

title: A Multimodal Machine Learning Framework Integrating Genomic, Epidemiological, Environmental, and Clinical Imaging Data for Accelerated Measles Detection and Transmission Inference
summary: Background: Measles resurged in the United States during 2025-2026, with more than 4,600 reported cases. Timely detection and transmission inference require integrated genomic, epidemiological, environmental, and clinical data. We developed a multimodal machine learning (ML) framework integrating genomic sequences, epidemiological indicators, wastewater surveillance, and clinical rash images. Methods: We evaluated a three-stage pipeline using public data. Stage 1 classified transmission linkage among 903 sequence pairs from the 2021 Ohio-Arizona-Washington outbreak using k-mer TF-IDF-SVD embeddings and pairwise single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) distances with leave-one-cluster-out cross-validation. Stage 2 predicted state-week outbreak risk using logistic regression and XGBoost with wastewater, mobility, and vaccination features under leave-one-year-out cross-validation. Stage 3 used BiomedCLIP ViT-B/16 embeddings and a fine-tuned multilayer perceptron for rash classification on MSLD v2.0 (755 images, 6 classes). InfoNCE contrastive learning aligned genomic and imaging embeddings. Results: Transmission-linkage classification achieved AUC 0.924 and F1 0.912 with logistic regression. Outbreak-risk prediction achieved AUC 0.707 with logistic regression across 2025-2026 leave-one-year-out folds. Contrastive alignment achieved Recall@1 = 0.985 on held-out paired data. Ablation showed genomic features dominated transmission-linkage prediction (genomic-only AUC 0.983), whereas wastewater positivity was the strongest outbreak-risk predictor (importance 0.402). Conclusions: Multimodal ML integrating genomic, epidemiological, wastewater, and clinical imaging data can support measles surveillance and transmission inference using public data. Prospective validation with paired clinical-genomic data, expanded wastewater coverage, and real-world workflows is needed before deployment.

AI.tldr: A study proposing a three-stage multimodal machine learning framework to enhance measles surveillance by integrating genomic, epidemiological, wastewater, and clinical imaging data.
AI.motivation: The resurgence of measles in the US (2025-2026) necessitates faster and more integrated detection methods beyond traditional clinical reporting.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline comprising: (1) Transmission linkage classification using genomic k-mer embeddings and SNP distances; (2) Outbreak risk prediction using logistic regression/XGBoost (wastewater, mobility, and vaccination data); and (3) Clinical rash classification using BiomedCLIP-based vision embeddings with InfoNCE contrastive learning to align genomic and image data.
AI.result: The model achieved high performance in transmission linkage (AUC 0.924) and high accuracy in clinical image-genomic alignment (Recall@1 = 0.985). Genomic data was the primary driver for linkage, while wastewater positivity was the most critical predictor for outbreak risk.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal integration significantly strengthens measles surveillance, though real-world deployment requires prospective validation with real-time clinical-genomic pairings.

title: ARMD-Predict: multi-site machine learning to predict antibiotic resistance before culture results
comment: 31 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables, 7 Extended Data figures, 5 Extended Data tables. Research web applications: this https URL
summary: Clinicians select empiric antibiotics before culture susceptibility results are available. Electronic health record (EHR) models could inform that choice, but most are developed at a single hospital and transport poorly to others. We developed ARMD-Predict using 7.5 million culture-antibiotic observations from four academic medical centers. One set of models estimates susceptibility to individual antibiotics; a second, hierarchical set predicts the infecting organism and then organism-specific resistance phenotypes. Across 23 pooled susceptibility models evaluated in same-period, patient-grouped test partitions, median area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.77 for inpatient urine and 0.70 for inpatient blood cultures; chronological retraining reduced AUROC by approximately 0.04. At an exploratory threshold with 95% positive predictive value, derived and evaluated on the same test observations, the model identified 55% of ceftriaxone-susceptible inpatient urine observations as suitable for narrower therapy and flagged 60% of ceftriaxone-resistant observations for broader coverage. Organism classifiers achieved top-3 accuracy of 51.3-83.3%; phenotype AUROCs were conditional on the observed organism. Research applications are available at this https URL. Independent calibration, threshold and end-to-end prospective validation are required before clinical use.

AI.tldr: The researchers developed **ARMD-Predict**, a multi-center machine learning framework designed to predict antibiotic susceptibility from EHR data to assist in empiric antibiotic selection.
AI.motivation: Current empiric antibiotic choices are often suboptimal because they rely on clinician intuition before culture results are ready. Existing EHR models suffer from poor generalizability (overfitting to single hospitals).
AI.method: The study utilized a large-scale dataset (7.5 million observations) from **four academic medical centers**. They implemented two modeling approaches: 1) Direct estimation of susceptibility to individual antibiotics, and 2) A hierarchical approach (predicting the organism first, then its specific resistance phenotype).
AI.result:
• **Performance:** Median AUROC of 0.77 for urine and 0.70 for blood cultures.
  • **Temporal Decay:** Model accuracy dropped by ~0.04 over time, indicating the need for retraining.
  • **Clinical Utility:** At a 95% PPV threshold, the model could identify 55% of cases suitable for narrowing therapy and 60% of cases requiring broader coverage.
  • **Organism Classification:** Top-3 accuracy ranged from 51.3% to 83.3%.
AI.conclusion: The model shows significant promise for multi-center application, but the authors emphasize that **prospective validation** and independent calibration are mandatory before clinical implementation.

title: An Exploratory Multiome Analysis of a BCG-Associated HSPC Signature: Trained-Immunity Marker in Blood and an Adverse Prognostic Association in Tumour
summary: Intravesical Bacillus Calmette--Guérin (BCG) is an established treatment for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC), and recent evidence indicates that bladder BCG induces transcriptional and chromatin changes in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs). However, the joint multi-omic structure of these BCG-associated changes and its potential to define transferable molecular signatures remain less well characterized. This study performed an exploratory integrative analysis of paired single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data from two NMIBC patients sampled before and after BCG treatment. Following preprocessing and barcode-level integration, 653 HSPCs were analysed using Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (MOFA+) with 2,000 HSPC-specific variable genes and 25,000 variable chromatin-accessibility peaks. Of ten latent factors, Factor~1 showed the strongest association with BCG status ($r=0.495$) and captured variation across both molecular views. RNA weights from Factor~1 were used to derive candidate gene signatures that showed partial consistency across patient-specific models. Cross-context evaluation showed associations with overall survival in TCGA-BLCA and recurrence in GSE199471, while a subset of signature genes showed consistent directional changes in monocytes following BCG vaccination in GSE184241. Together, these findings identify a candidate multi-omic axis associated with BCG exposure and suggest that its derived molecular signatures exhibit context-dependent behaviour across distinct biological and clinical settings.

AI.tldr: The study identifies a specific multi-omic molecular signature in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) that changes in response to BCG treatment for bladder cancer.
AI.motivation: While BCG treatment is standard for NMIBC and known to affect HSPCs, the integrated relationship between transcriptional (RNA) and epigenetic (ATAC) changes remains poorly understood.
AI.method: The researchers performed paired single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq on HSPCs from NMIBC patients before and after BCG treatment. They used Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (MOFA+) to integrate 2,000 genes and 25,000 chromatin peaks.
AI.result: A single latent factor (Factor 1) strongly correlated with BCG status ($r=0.495$). This factor captured integrated variation across both RNA and chromatin accessibility. The resulting gene signatures showed clinical relevance, correlating with overall survival (TCGA-BLCA) and recurrence (GSE199471).
AI.conclusion: The study identifies a multi-omic axis triggered by BCG exposure that exhibits consistent, though context-dependent, behavior across different clinical and biological datasets.

title: Canonical residual physics-informed neural networks and algorithmic perturbation landscapes map cell-fate transitions in longitudinal H3K27M glioma
comment: 18 pages
summary: Pediatric high-grade glioma is a dynamically heterogeneous disease in which therapeutic selection pressures, microenvironmental selection and developmental plasticity can reorganize cellular-state structure over time. Here we investigated these adaptive behaviors in glioma dynamics from single-cell ecologies by merging physics-driven artificial intelligence and complex systems theory. Specifically, this study explores canonical residual-based physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), dynamical systems modelling comparators, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and Block Decomposition Method (BDM) perturbation analysis to understand glioma cell fate decisions. The primary analyses distinguished longitudinal initial from recurrent H3K27M cells and, within the recurrent specimen set, stem/progenitor-like from differentiated/glial-like annotation-derived states. Across five-fold cross-validation, RD achieved AUC $0.995 \pm 0.005$ and macro-F1 $0.973 \pm 0.016$ for initial--recurrence discrimination, and AUC $0.698 \pm 0.012$ and macro-F1 $0.629 \pm 0.014$ for recurrent-state subtype discrimination. FP achieved AUC $0.931 \pm 0.018$ and $0.665 \pm 0.012$, respectively. Cross-model XAI repeatedly prioritized PTGDS, CHI3L1, IGFBP7, SPARCL1 and NRXN3 in longitudinal progression. BDM perturbation rankings emphasized heat-shock/stress-response and immune-associated network signatures. These findings are candidate computational network biomarkers rather than experimentally established causal signatures. The study provides a reproducible bridge between physics-constrained latent dynamics, interpretable gene attribution, and data-driven algorithmic perturbation landscapes for in silico pattern generation about glioma cell fate plasticity and early recurrence detection.

AI.tldr: The study utilizes a hybrid framework of physics-informed AI and complex systems theory to model the cellular evolution and plasticity of pediatric high-grade glioma (pHGG) from single-cell data.
AI.motivation: To understand how therapeutic pressures and microenvironmental factors drive cellular state changes and recurrence in pHGG through the lens of dynamical systems.
AI.method: The researchers combined Residual-based Physics-Informed Neural Networks (RD-PINNs), dynamical systems modeling, Explainable AI (XAI), and the Block Decomposition Method (BDM) to analyze single-cell ecologies.
AI.result: The RD model outperformed the FP model in discriminating between initial and recurrent cells (AUC 0.995) and recurrent subtypes (AUC 0.698). XAI identified key genes (PTGDS, CHI3L1, etc.) involved in progression, while BDM highlighted stress-response and immune-related networks.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a reproducible method for linking physics-constrained latent dynamics with gene attribution, offering potential computational biomarkers for early recurrence detection and studying cell fate plasticity.

title: Debate, Not Voting: Agentic Arbitration over Weak Optical Chemical Structure Recognition Models
summary: Optical chemical structure recognition (OCSR) turns a picture of a molecule into a machine-readable string, and it stands between decades of printed chemistry and any computational use. On real documents individual models remain unreliable. Over a 1000-molecule sample of MolParser, three readers score $46.0\%$, $43.4\%$ and $42.4\%$ exact match, yet at least one of them is right on $60.8\%$ of molecules. That gap is an ensembling problem, but not one voting can solve, because the readers seldom agree and seldom err together. We place the readers inside a multi-agent scaffold. Four language-model agents with cheminformatics tools argue about a candidate structure, write findings to an append-only knowledge base, and are held to render-and-compare gates that admit a correction only when it is demonstrably better. The debate reaches $61.9\%$, beating the best single reader by $15.9$ points and plurality voting by $9.2$ points ($p<10^{-9}$ for both, robust to correction for all $27$ tests we report), and is indistinguishable from the any-reader-right ceiling. That aggregate hides two opposing effects. On the $661$ molecules with no stereochemistry the debate is $3.9$ points above the ceiling ($p=0.004$), constructing structures no reader proposed, while on the $339$ stereochemical ones it falls below. We then swap the arbitrating model. A stronger arbitrator adds $2.2$ points (nominal $p=0.039$; neither this nor the $+3.9$ survives Bonferroni correction over all $27$ tests, so both are suggestive), and its mechanism is visible: it opens a correction on $423$ of $1000$ molecules against $120$, and an interaction test indicates it depends less on the readers (nominal $p=0.018$, not correction-robust). We conclude that the useful unit of progress is the arbitration policy rather than the reader, and that OCSR accuracy is better read against the union oracle than against the best single model.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent scaffold using LLMs and cheminformatics tools improves Optical Chemical Structure Recognition (OCSR) accuracy by debating candidate structures, reaching performance levels comparable to the union of all individual readers.
AI.motivation: Individual OCSR models are unreliable on real documents, and simple voting fails to improve accuracy because readers often disagree or err independently.
AI.method: A multi-agent system where four LLM agents argue about chemical structures, use cheminformatics tools, record findings in an append-only knowledge base, and are subject to ''render-and-compare' gates for corrections.
AI.result: The debate method achieved 61.9% exact match accuracy, outperforming the best single reader by 15.9 points and plurality voting by 9.2 points, reaching the 'any-reader-right' ceiling on non-stereochemical molecules.
AI.conclusion: Progress in OCSR should be measured by the effectiveness of arbitration policies rather than individual readers, as the arbiter can synthesize correct structures that no single reader proposed.

title: TargetAgent: Mathematical AI Co-Scientist for Drug Target Identification
summary: Given the challenges of pharmaceutical development, there is increasing interest in computational approaches for identifying novel drug targets. Transcriptomics technologies enable the analysis of disease mechanisms at unprecedented resolution, while spatially resolved platforms further preserve the spatial organization of cells within tissues, allowing analysis to focus on specific regions of disease localization. To derive actionable therapeutic targets from these data, it is necessary to identify mechanisms that recur across a population rather than those observed in individual patients, which requires integrated analysis across disease conditions and donor cohorts. Here, we present the groundwork for an AI co-scientist framework for the sequential analysis of multi-batch spatial transcriptomics data that integrates interpretable mathematical models, including optimal transport, tensor factorizations, and topological data analysis, with LLM-powered agentic interpretation. Leveraging the complementary information provided by these mathematical models, the agents sequentially identify regions in which the disease is localized, molecular targets within these regions, and the direction in which each target should be modulated. Applied as a proof of concept to a public Stereo-seq study of the Alzheimer's disease (AD)-affected prefrontal cortex, we demonstrate that the agents converge on the white matter as the primary locus of the moderate-disease signal and identify a loss of myelin programme usage despite increasing oligodendrocyte abundance. The agents subsequently propose 29 candidate therapeutic targets, led by an oligodendrocyte differentiation module on which multiple mathematical perspectives converge, and flag 20 genes whose relevance to AD has not been previously reported. These results are hypothesis-generating and motivate further validation in larger, independent cohorts.

AI.tldr: An AI co-scientist framework for multi-batch spatial transcriptomics that integrates mathematical models (optimal transport, tensor factorization, TDA) with LLM agents to identify disease-localized molecular targets.
AI.motivation: The need for scalable, integrated computational approaches to identify recurring therapeutic targets across patient cohorts using high-resolution spatial transcriptomics data.
AI.method: A sequential analysis framework combining interpretable mathematical models—optimal transport, tensor factorizations, and topological data analysis—with LLM-powered agentic interpretation.
AI.result: Applied to Alzheimer's disease Stereo-seq data, the system identified the white matter as the primary disease locus, identified a loss of myelin program usage, and proposed 29 candidate targets, including 20 novel genes.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a powerful hypothesis-generating tool for drug target identification, though it requires further validation in larger, independent cohorts.

title: RADAgent: Automating RADseq Pipelines with Private Open-Source LLMs
comment: Accepted at IEEE BIBM 2026. Code: this https URL
summary: Restriction site-associated DNA sequencing (RADseq) is a family of reduced-representation sequencing methods. It uses restriction enzymes to sample subsets of the genome, therefore allowing multiple individuals to be sequenced and genotyped together at low cost. RADseq is widely used for population genomics, evolutionary biology, marker discovery, and the development of SNP panels, but complete analysis still requires expert coordination across multiple tools and processing stages. Traditional RADseq analysis requires expert coordination of heterogeneous bioinformatics tools, intermediate artifacts, quality-control checks, and parameter-dependent decisions across multiple stages. Although individual steps can be scripted, executing the complete workflow still requires human oversight for state tracking, result validation, and failure handling. To automate this expert-driven coordination, we present RADAgent, which introduces a modular agentic method for reliable RADseq workflow execution with an open-weight LLM. RADAgent maps the natural boundaries of the RADseq workflow into 16 independently executable and verifiable agent modules and uses a model-independent runtime for bounded tool execution, on-disk verification, and failure recovery. We evaluate RADAgent on a real population-genomics dataset containing 476 samples from 19 populations. The results demonstrate that RADAgent reliably automates the complete RADseq workflow with an open-weight LLM while keeping genomic data and model execution within the local computing environment. The code is publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces **RADAgent**, an automated, modular framework that uses an open-weight Large Language Model (LLM) to manage the complex, multi-stage bioinformatics workflow of RADseq (Restriction site-associated DNA sequencing).
AI.motivation: Traditional RADseq analysis is error-prone and labor-intensive, requiring manual coordination of heterogeneous tools, constant quality control, and expert decision-making to handle parameter dependencies and failures.
AI.method: RADAgent decomposes the RADseq workflow into **16 independent, verifiable agent modules**. It utilizes a model-independent runtime to ensure bounded tool execution, on-disk verification, and automated failure recovery, all while maintaining data privacy by running locally.
AI.result: The framework was validated on a large-scale population genomics dataset (476 samples, 19 populations), proving it can reliably automate the end-to-end process without sending sensitive genomic data to external APIs.
AI.conclusion: RADAgent demonstrates that agentic LLM methods can successfully automate complex scientific workflows while ensuring reproducibility and data security in local computing environments.

title: Cohort Effects, Not Treatment Response, Dominate Public Immunotherapy Cohorts: Evidence from Microbiome and Tumor Genomic Data
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 13 tables. Extended version of a paper accepted to the IEEE BIBM 2026 Workshop Proceedings. Code: this https URL
summary: Researchers often pool public gut microbiome datasets from immunotherapy studies to get around small sample sizes, assuming that adding cohorts adds statistical power faster than it adds differences between studies. We test that assumption. We processed four public shotgun metagenomic cohorts of patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade through one pipeline and pooled them step by step, from 39 to 283 patients. Because the PERMANOVA effect size R^2 is above zero even when there is no real effect, we compared every result with its exact chance expectation. Measured as raw variance explained, cohort membership accounted for 8 to 27 times more variance than treatment response, although much of that ratio comes from sample size alone. At every pooling step, treatment response explained no more variance than chance (within 0.2 percentage points) and was never significant, while cohort membership explained 6.0 to 9.5 percentage points beyond chance (p = 0.001 each time). Classification stayed at chance across three model types, none of six leak-free batch-correction strategies recovered signal, and no genus reached significance in a random-effects meta-analysis. The largest single cohort (n = 165) was also non-significant, although simulation shows it had at least 90% power to detect an effect at its own 95% upper bound; within it, recruiting site alone explained 7.0 percentage points beyond chance. In three tumor genomic cohorts (n = 223), a small but real response effect sat next to a cohort effect about eighteen times larger, so the problem is not specific to microbiome data. We release batch_detector, an open tool that reports chance-corrected cohort and response effects before pooling, and test it on an independent colorectal cancer meta-analysis.

AI.tldr: The study warns that pooling disparate microbiome datasets to increase statistical power is often ineffective and misleading because inter-study (cohort) variation drastically outweighs treatment effects.
AI.motivation: Researchers frequently pool public datasets to overcome small sample sizes, assuming that increased $N$ provides more signal than noise/batch effects.
AI.method: The authors pooled four shotgun metagenomic cohorts (n=39 to 283) using a single pipeline and applied a 'chance-corrected' PERMANOVA to distinguish real signal from statistical artifacts.
AI.result: 1. Cohort membership explained 8–27x more variance than treatment response. 2. Treatment response effects were statistically indistinguishable from chance. 3. Batch-correction methods failed to recover any treatment signal. 4. The phenomenon was also observed in tumor genomic cohorts, indicating a broader issue in meta-analyses.
AI.conclusion: Pooling datasets without accounting for significant batch effects can lead to false conclusions. The authors released `batch_detector` to help researchers quantify cohort vs. response effects before pooling.

title: Physiology as Topology: Intervenable Organ Graphs for Longitudinal Patient Forecasting
summary: Do language models forecast patient trajectories by reasoning through physiology, or by fitting surface statistics? We introduce PhysioCircuit, a multi-agent agent system that represents each organ as an agent and each physiological relation as an editable mechanism card with direction, lag, and evidence. Its expert-defined graph is frozen at inference, enabling controlled edge interventions. We also introduce PhysioCircuit-Bench, a mechanism-controlled benchmark spanning three organ systems, treatment events, and real ICU admissions. We evaluate intervention-direction agreement (IDAR), which requires the affected organ to change in the expected direction within the expected lag window. The expert graph substantially outperforms all topology controls on edge-IDAR, including fully connected, random, and reversed graphs. Independent clinician adjudication supports the counterfactual results. PhysioCircuit transfers to new organ systems by configuration alone, without retraining, while preserving inspectable and editable relations.

AI.tldr: PhysioCircuit is a multi-agent system using an expert-defined physiological graph to test if language models reason through physiology rather than just statistical patterns.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether language models forecast patient trajectories through physiological reasoning or by merely fitting surface statistics.
AI.method: The authors introduce PhysioCircuit, a multi-agent system where organs are agents and physiological relations are editable mechanism cards. They also introduce PhysioCircuit-Bench, a mechanism-controlled benchmark used to evaluate models via intervention-direction agreement (IDAR).
AI.result: PhysioCircuit's expert graph architecture achieves higher IDAR than fully connected, random, or reversed graphs, with results validated by clinician adjudication.
AI.conclusion: The expert-defined graph structure significantly outperforms random topologies in intervention-direction agreement, and the system demonstrates zero-shot transferability to new organ systems by configuration alone.

title: Duration-Aware World Models for Sleep Staging with Dwell-Time Constraints
comment: 16 pages, 7 figures
summary: Closed-loop neuromodulation requires sleep staging that respects stage-specific minimum dwells: stimulation policies switch by sleep stage, and a policy change is permitted only after the current stage has persisted for its minimum duration. Discriminative classifiers fragment stage trajectories---for example, a 30 s Wake segment inside a 10 min N2 run---and even hidden semi-Markov smoothing leaves 11.3% of segments below the minimum dwell threshold. This paper presents a world model in which a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) learns dwell structure endogenously from EEG, via duration-aware latent sampling, a survival-curve dwell prior, and transition-matrix calibration, and a trajectory-level hard-constraint layer guarantees the minimum dwell at decoding. On SHHS-1 (200 subjects, 160/20/20, three repeated splits), the model reaches a test accuracy of 0.690 +/- 0.053 (95% CI over 3 folds) versus 0.641 +/- 0.042 for an identically split discriminative baseline, with macro-F1 +17.5 pp and better accuracy on all three folds. On Sleep-EDF the constraint layer cuts below-threshold segments from 71.8% to 0.1% with no accuracy loss (0.734 to 0.737), and an online locked scheduler reduces RL policy switches by 87% per night while keeping every policy run at least 90 s. To the best of the author's knowledge, this is the first system to couple learned dwell statistics with a decoding-time hard guarantee. Code and pretrained weights will be released.

AI.tldr: A new RSSM-based world model for sleep staging that learns dwell durations and uses a hard-constraint layer to ensure minimum stage durations, preventing fragmented trajectories in closed-loop neuromodulation.
AI.motivation: Closed-loop neuromodulation requires sleep staging that respects minimum dwell times, but standard discriminative classifiers produce fragmented stage trajectories that violate these constraints.
AI.method: A world model using a Recurrent State-Space Model (RSSM) that learns dwell structure via duration-aware latent sampling, survival-curve dwell priors, and transition-matrix calibration, combined with a trajectory-level hard-constraint layer for decoding.
AI.result: The model achieved 0.690 accuracy on SHHS-1 (outperforming discriminative baselines) and reduced below-threshold segments on Sleep-EDF from 71.8% to 0.1% while reducing RL policy switches by 87%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed system is the first to couple learned dwell statistics with a decoding-time hard guarantee, successfully reducing policy switches and preventing sub-threshold segments without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Agent-guided epitope excision enables economical de novo binder design
comment: Co-corresponding authors: Jun W. Kim and Annalisa Pawlosky. 24 pages, 6 main figures, 1 main table, 5 supporting figures, 1 supporting table
summary: De novo protein design campaigns remain bottlenecked by the inference compute time required to generate and rank candidates, limiting wider functional exploration. Here, we introduce and evaluate an epitope excision approach that truncates targets to local interface windows to accelerate both backbone diffusion and structure prediction. Across 15 targets and 3,666 designs, excised windows closely reproduced full-target binding interfaces (median C\alpha RMSD of 0.37 Å) and made it practical to design binders against the 719-residue extracellular domain of fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP) by cutting RFdiffusion and AlphaFold3 GPU time by ~ 88% in one of the epitopes. Pairing this workflow with an agentic optimization loop allowed the system to autonomously identify catalytic-site targeting strategies. Under a fixed compute budget, a human-in-the-loop (HITL) workflow raised the computational hit rate from 5.06% to 9.33% while further cutting GPU hours by ~ 42%. We also found that omitting target multiple sequence alignments during refolding roughly substantially increased the apparent yield. Wet-lab validation with yeast display identified nanomolar binders from the generated designs with the HITL and the fully autonomous agent (human-out-of-the-loop, HOOTL) arms recovering more enriched designs than the PI-alone baseline. Together, target excision and agent-guided search offer a practical way to scale de novo binder design to large, therapeutically relevant proteins.

AI.tldr: By focusing computation on local binding sites (excision) and using AI agents to optimize search strategies, the authors significantly accelerate and improve the success rate of designing binders for large therapeutic proteins.
AI.motivation: Standard de novo protein design is limited by the high computational cost (inference time) required by diffusion models (e.g., RFdiffusion) and structure predictors (e.g., AlphaFold) when dealing with large, complex proteins.
AI.method: The authors propose an 'epitope excision' approach, which involves truncating large protein targets into smaller, local interface windows. This is combined with an agentic optimization loop (incorporating both Human-in-the-Loop and Human-out-of-the-Loop models) to autonomously guide the design process.
AI.result:
1. **Efficiency**: Cutting target windows reduced GPU time by ~88% for large targets like FAP. 
2. **Accuracy**: Truncated windows maintained high fidelity to full targets (median Cα RMSD of 0.37 Å). 
3. **Performance**: A Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) workflow nearly doubled the computational hit rate (from 5.06% to 9.33%) while reducing GPU usage by 42%. 
4. **Validation**: Wet-lab yeast display confirmed the discovery of nanomolar binders, with agentic workflows outperforming manual (PI-alone) baselines.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a highly efficient workflow for de novo protein binder design that addresses the computational bottleneck of large protein targets through 'epitope excision' and agentic automation.

title: Multiscale Topology-Regulated Nonlinear Dynamics for Protein B-Factor Prediction and Single-Cell Type Classification
summary: Protein B-factor prediction and single-cell type classification are important for characterizing structural variability and cellular heterogeneity, with applications in biological function analysis and drug discovery. However, static geometric descriptors do not directly capture how multiscale connectivity shapes responses to local perturbations. Here, we introduce multiscale graph-coupled Burgers response learning (MGCBRL), a framework integrating algebraic topology and nonlinear dynamics to construct predictive biological representations. Specifically, a filtration converts protein coordinates or cellular principal component scores into weighted graphs at ten neighborhood scales. Independent unit impulses initiate node-specific responses governed by nonlinear Burgers dynamics. Statistical summaries or sampled source-node trajectories then encode the influence of structural neighborhoods on transient signal evolution. The simulated responses serve as computational probes rather than models of biological motion. For cross-protein prediction, multiscale response statistics are combined with spectral perturbation descriptors measuring changes in Laplacian spectra after node removal. For single-cell classification, principal component scores augment these features to retain explicit expression-space information, and the resulting descriptors support downstream supervised learning. Across 104 proteins and 13 single-cell datasets, MGCBRL achieved configuration-selected mean scores of 0.888 for within-protein Pearson correlation and 0.950 for transductive cell classification balanced accuracy, with leave-one-protein-out mean correlations of 0.496-0.558. Our framework provides a shared strategy for transforming multiscale biological connectivity into informative response descriptors, supporting predictive analysis of protein structures and transcriptomic profiles.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces **MGCBRL** (Multiscale Graph-Coupled Burgers Response Learning), a framework that uses algebraic topology and nonlinear dynamics to transform biological data (protein structures and single-cell transcriptomics) into predictive descriptors.
AI.motivation: Static geometric descriptors fail to capture how multiscale connectivity influences responses to local perturbations, limiting their effectiveness in modeling structural variability and cellular heterogeneity.
AI.method: 1. **Filtration**: Converts protein coordinates or cell PCA scores into weighted graphs across 10 neighborhood scales. 2. **Burgers Dynamics**: Applies nonlinear Burgers equations to simulate signal evolution from node-specific impulses. 3. **Feature Engineering**: Combines statistical summaries of these transient responses with spectral perturbation descriptors (Laplacian spectra changes).
AI.result: Demonstrated high performance across 104 proteins and 13 single-cell datasets, achieving 0.888 Pearson correlation for protein B-factors and 0.950 balanced accuracy for single-cell classification.
AI.conclusion: MGCBRL provides a robust strategy for converting complex biological connectivity into informative, dynamic descriptors for downstream machine learning tasks.

title: ProtAgent: Post-Training Compact Protein Tool Agents with Interaction-Level Credit Assignment
comment: 20 pages, 2 figures
summary: Protein annotation agents must choose suitable bioinformatics tools, interpret their outputs, and use the resulting evidence in the final answer. Most existing systems rely on frontier-scale models. We ask whether a compact model can instead learn this behavior through post-training with real tool interaction. We present ProtAgent, a two-stage pipeline that uses supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the tool interface and standard on-policy REINFORCE to improve the interaction policy. Intermediate tool calls receive action rewards, and the final response receives a terminal answer reward. Step-level returns assign these rewards to the responses that produced them and to preceding actions. The episode-level baseline instead assigns one episode return to every action. On a fixed closed-loop protocol with real bioinformatics tools, ProtAgent-8B achieves 61.00% success under the annotation-coverage metric, compared with 41.60% for DeepSeek-V3.2-Thinking 671B and 60.80% for the strongest evaluated frontier system. In the three-seed comparison, mean success is 42.70% with episode-level returns and 61.40% with step-level returns under identity return normalization; the corresponding group-relative results are 36.50% and 58.20%. The metric measures recovery of reference annotations under this protocol; it does not by itself establish biological correctness or complete evidence grounding.

AI.tldr: ProtAgent is a compact 8B parameter model that outperforms frontier-scale models in protein annotation tasks by using a two-stage training pipeline consisting of supervised fine-tuning and on-policy reinforcement learning with step-level rewards.
AI.motivation: Existing protein annotation systems rely on massive frontier-scale models, raising the question of whether compact models can achieve similar or better performance through specialized post-training focused on real tool interaction.
AI.method: The authors propose a two-stage pipeline: 1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) to learn tool interfaces, and 2) on-policy REINFORCE reinforcement learning. They implement a reward system using both action rewards for intermediate tool calls and terminal rewards for final answers, comparing step-level reward assignment against episode-level baseline assignment.
AI.result: ProtAgent-8B achieved a 61.00% success rate under the annotation-coverage metric, surpassing DeepSeek-V3.2-Thinking 671B (41.60%) and matching the strongest evaluated frontier system (60.80%). Step-level returns significantly outperformed episode-level returns.
AI.conclusion: Compact models can effectively learn complex bioinformatics tool interaction policies through targeted reinforcement learning, achieving performance parity with much larger models in protein annotation tasks.

title: MechGate: combining mechanism-derived measures of permeation and efflux to screen small molecule drugs targeting Escherichia coli
comment: 35 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables, including supplementary material
summary: Most antibiotic molecules must cross the cell membrane and escape efflux pumps before hitting their targets. For de novo antibiotic design, very few of the in-silico-generated drug molecules can successfully pass these two steps. Existing evaluations of generated molecules do not separate these steps. Therefore, we introduce MechGate, a mechanism-resolved screening tool evaluating small drug molecules against E. coli, measuring permeation, efflux and antibacterial activity. After SMILES input, five measures are reported side by side: two for permeation via porins, one for permeation via the phospholipid membrane, one for efflux and one for activity. Each measure is read on its own, so a molecule that fails can be traced to the step that stops it. All features are taken from papers that state their mechanism rather than selected by importance ranking. On an external set of marketed antibacterials the measures give a precision of 0.789 to 0.873 against baselines near 0.44, and combining them the way the mechanism predicts raises precision to 0.92. We also find that the four public source libraries are separable from one another using physicochemical features alone; every measure here therefore draws both classes from a single library. All code is open-source and requires no commercial software.

AI.tldr: MechGate provides a high-precision, open-source diagnostic tool that identifies exactly *why* a generated antibiotic molecule fails (permeation vs. efflux vs. activity).
AI.motivation: Most antibiotic failures in silico occur because molecules cannot effectively cross cell membranes or escape efflux pumps. Current evaluation methods lack the granularity to pinpoint which specific biological barrier is causing a molecule to fail.
AI.method: Unlike existing tools that provide a single efficacy score, MechGate employs a **mechanism-resolved approach**. It evaluates molecules across five distinct, independent parameters: porin permeation (2 metrics), phospholipid membrane permeation, efflux resistance, and antibacterial activity. These features are derived from validated mechanistic literature rather than mere statistical importance.
AI.result: MechGate demonstrates high predictive accuracy. On marketed antibacterials, it achieved a precision of **0.789–0.873**, significantly outperforming baselines (~0.44). When all mechanistic measures are combined according to biological pathways, precision increases to **0.92**.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces **MechGate**, a novel screening tool designed to overcome a major gap in *de novo* antibiotic design: the failure to distinguish between different barriers to drug efficacy.

title: Sensorimotor behaviour from an untrained brain-and-nerve-cord connectome
comment: 42 pages: the manuscript with six figures, and the Supplementary Information (4 figures, 8 tables) appended
summary: Connectomes now map the neurons and synapses of an adult fly's brain and nerve cord, but how much of behaviour follows from the wiring is unknown. Here we turn one such connectome into a spiking network of 172,433 neurons with a published brain model's untuned parameters, and run it alone and inside a simulated body. Two fixed rules join them: odours and looming objects drive sensory neurons, and motor neurons move the legs. Alone, the network passes a signal to the motor neurons it is known to drive when the pathway supplies about 2% or more of their input. In the body, the fly navigates around obstacles to 95% of the odour sources. A rewiring that keeps each neuron's connection counts and signs reaches 18%, and the fly's leg commands replayed with the senses off reach almost none, so navigation needs the measured wiring and sensory feedback. Dopamine-gated weakening of the mushroom body's output synapses turns approach to an odour into avoidance, which requires the pairing and is odour-specific once one olfactory synapse class is scaled. An untrained connectome thus supports a behaviour and its learned reversal, and the pathways it cannot drive mark what the diagram leaves out.

AI.tldr: Researchers successfully transformed a physical connectome (a map of neural connections) into a functional, spiking computational model to test if brain wiring alone can drive complex behaviors.
AI.motivation: To determine how much of an organism's behavior is dictated by its physical neural architecture (the connectome) versus other unknown factors.
AI.method: The team converted a fruit fly connectome into a network of 172,433 spiking neurons. This network was tested in two modes: as an isolated network and embedded within a simulated physical body with sensory inputs (odors, looming objects) and motor outputs (leg movement).
AI.result:
1. **Functional Navigation**: The model successfully navigated to 95% of odor sources and avoided obstacles.
2. **Structural Necessity**: Rewiring just 18% of the connections destroyed the behavior, proving the specific wiring is critical.
3. **Learning Capability**: By simulating dopamine-gated synaptic weakening in the mushroom body, the model demonstrated
AI.conclusion: An untrained, raw connectome is sufficient to support both innate navigation and learned behaviors (like odor avoidance). This validates the connectome as a foundational blueprint for behavior, while noting that missing pathways in the map highlight gaps in our current biological knowledge.

title: Benchmarking miRNA Target Prediction Methods
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM 2026)
summary: Background: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate gene expression by binding to target mRNAs. Although many tools predict miRNA-target interactions, predictions show limited concordance, and benchmarks relying on curated databases may be biased by overlap with tool-development data. Methods: We benchmarked seven tools (TargetScan, miRDB, miRmap, DIANA-microT, RNA22, miRWalk, and mirDIP) across approximately 59.7 million candidate miRNA-mRNA pairs. Each pair received an evidence-graded reference score (0-3) combining validated interactions from miRTarBase and TarBase with expression-derived evidence from paired miRNA-seq and mRNA-seq data in an induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) cohort of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome and control lines. Performance was evaluated using Type I error, statistical power, and false discovery proportion (FDP). Robustness was assessed by increasing reference-score stringency (truth signal) and including progressively lower-confidence predictions (model signal). Optimal cutoffs maximized Youden's J statistic. Results: Rankings were largely consistent across settings. TargetScan and miRDB maintained Type I error rates below 0.05, with TargetScan showing the lowest FDP, but both had limited power. mirDIP achieved the highest power at the cost of the highest Type I error rate. At optimal cutoffs, mirDIP best balanced sensitivity and specificity (Youden's J = 0.566), followed by DIANA-microT (J = 0.481); miRWalk and RNA22 had FDPs near the random-prediction baseline. No tool was optimal across all metrics; tool and cutoff selection should reflect whether sensitivity or specificity is prioritized."""

AI.tldr: A large-scale benchmarking study of seven miRNA-target prediction tools using a novel, evidence-graded reference standard to evaluate accuracy and reliability.
AI.motivation: Existing miRNA-target prediction tools show poor concordance, and current benchmarks are often biased because they rely on curated databases that overlap with the training data used to develop the tools.
AI.method: The researchers evaluated seven tools (TargetScan, miRDB, miRmap, DIANA-microT, RNA22, miRWalk, and mirDIP) against 59.7 million pairs. They created a unique reference score (0-3) by combining validated databases (miRTarBase/TarBase) with real-world expression data from iPSC cohorts (22q11.2 deletion syndrome). Performance was measured via Type I error, statistical power, and False Discovery Proportion (FDP).
AI.result: No single tool outperformed others in all categories. TargetScan and miRDB were highly conservative (low Type I error/FDP but low power), while mirDIP provided the highest sensitivity (power) but higher Type I error. mirDIP achieved the best overall balance (highest Youden's J = 0.566).
AI.conclusion: Tool selection should be application-specific: use TargetScan/miRDB when avoiding false positives is critical, and mirDIP when maximizing discovery (sensitivity) is the priority.

title: Tau creates spatially moving hotspots of amyloid-$β$ secondary nucleation: a reaction-diffusion model
summary: Tau-amyloid-$\beta$ cross-seeding creates a spatial paradox. Bioavailable tau can promote A$\beta$42 nucleation, thereby increasing local fibril number and catalytic-site burden; yet the same fibrils consume the free A$\beta$ monomer required for homotypic secondary nucleation. The region containing the most tau or fibrillar material therefore need not be the region with the highest secondary-nucleation rate. We test this idea with a reaction-diffusion model that tracks a propagating effective tau catalyst, free A$\beta$ monomer, elongation-competent fibrils, fibril mass, and the catalytic sites exposed to monomer. The model reduces the spatial competition to two quantities: accessible catalytic sites and free monomer. Their balance yields an exact condition for an interior kinetic maximum: the logarithmic decrease in accessible catalytic sites must equal twice the logarithmic increase in free monomer. Two Damkohler numbers then separate the relevant competitions-elongation versus clearance, and elongation versus diffusive redistribution-while a monomer screening length sets the physical scale over which depletion can persist. Independent transport and turnover estimates place this length near 0.44-0.54 mm. Simulations show that tau first raises secondary nucleation near its source; continued fibril growth then produces a monomer-depleted wake, and the maximum shifts to a region with fewer catalytic sites but more available monomer. Oligomer transport and sustained reversible exchange can weaken or eliminate this contrast, whereas growth-history-dependent site density can strengthen it. The robust prediction is therefore a spatial separation among tau burden, fibril-mass growth, and instantaneous A$\beta$ secondary-nucleation activity, rather than a universal hotspot speed.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a 'spatial paradox' in Alzheimer's pathology, where the highest density of Tau or Aβ fibrils does not necessarily coincide with the highest rate of new Aβ nucleation due to monomer depletion.
AI.motivation: To explain the apparent mismatch between the location of protein aggregates (Tau/Aβ) and the actual sites of active secondary nucleation.
AI.method: A reaction-diffusion mathematical model tracking five key variables: effective tau catalyst, free Aβ monomer, elongation-competent fibrils, fibril mass, and exposed catalytic sites.
AI.result: The study identifies a competition between 'accessible catalytic sites' and 'free monomer.' It defines a mathematical condition for a kinetic maximum and introduces two Damkohler numbers to characterize the competition between reaction and diffusion/clearance.
AI.conclusion: Fibril growth creates a 'monomer-depleted wake.' Consequently, the peak of secondary nucleation shifts away from the Tau source to a region with fewer fibrils but higher monomer availability. This predicts a spatial separation between Tau burden, fibril mass, and active nucleation sites.

title: New developments in the geometry and topology of 3D head-direction coding
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures
summary: The head-direction (HD) system is a neuronal compass that represents head orientation in 3D. Its encoding of 3D head orientation can be decomposed into a multiplexed representation of 2D head tilt relative to gravity and 1D head orientation in the horizontal plane (azimuth). Defining azimuth during 3D motion is not trivial, and recent studies have indicated that the HD system implements a so-called dual-axis/tilted-azimuth (DA/TA) rule, a representation that is well supported experimentally but remains mathematically and mechanistically difficult to interpret. Here, I introduce a new formulation of DA/TA based directly on the elements of a rotation matrix describing 3D head orientation. In this formulation, TA is represented by a 2D vector, whose direction encode TA and whose norm depends on tilt, consistent with a tilt-dependent gain of HD tuning reported by experimental studies. I provide a geometrical interpretation of this formulation and use it to characterize the topology of the resulting representation. More generally, I introduce a framework in which head orientation is represented by a rotation matrix and neuronal responses arise from linear combinations of its elements followed by nonlinear transformations. Within this framework, the linear stage specifies which aspects of 3D orientation are encoded, and therefore allow relating neuronal representation to linear algebra concepts. Classical HD tuning, gravity tuning, and DA/TA can all be described within this common framework. Together, these results provide a new mathematical, geometrical, and topological perspective on 3D HD coding.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new mathematical framework to explain how the brain's head-direction (HD) system encodes 3D head orientation, specifically resolving the complexities of the 'dual-axis/tilted-azimuth' (DA/TA) rule.
AI.motivation: While the HD system's 3D encoding can be split into 2D tilt and 1D azimuth, the current 'DA/TA' rule used to describe this is mathematically difficult to interpret and lacks a clear mechanistic basis.
AI.method: The author moves away from traditional geometric descriptions and instead derives the HD representation directly from the elements of a **3D rotation matrix**. They propose a two-stage model: 1) a **linear stage** (where neurons respond to linear combinations of rotation matrix elements) and 2) a **nonlinear stage** (the final tuning curve).
AI.result: The new formulation represents Tilted Azimuth (TA) as a 2D vector where the direction encodes the azimuth and the norm depends on the head tilt. This successfully unifies classical HD tuning, gravity tuning, and the DA/TA rule into a single, coherent algebraic framework.
AI.conclusion: This approach provides a rigorous mathematical, geometrical, and topological foundation for understanding 3D neural coding, making it easier to relate biological neuronal responses to linear algebra.

title: The dominance of feedback mechanisms for perception in the central visual field: the flip tilt illusion by backward masking and the Feedforward-Feedback-Verify-reWeight algorithm
comment: 30 pages, 9 figures, it is also available at this https URL
summary: The flip tilt illusion is the misperception of the orientation of the alignment between a pair of dots by 90 degrees. It occurs when the dot-pair contains one black dot and one white dot, is typically visible only in the peripheral visual field. It is predicted by the central-peripheral dichotomy (CPD) theory. Along the visual pathway from retina to downstream stages, our brain admits only a tiny fraction of visual input information for recognition due to a processing bottleneck that starts from the output of the primary visual cortex (V1) along the visual pathway. Accordingly, perception downstream from V1 relies on impoverished information, selected largely by gaze shifts to center the selected content at fovea and additionally by the capacity of the bottleneck even in the central visual field, likely making perceptual hypotheses about the visual scene ambiguous or illusory. To overcome, downstream areas send feedback to upstream areas such as V1 to query for additional information, thereby re-assessing the weights of the initial hypotheses. This perceptual algorithm is termed Feedforward-Feedback-Verify-reWeight (FFVW). To save resources, the feedback query is limited largely to the central visual field. The peripheral visual field is thus vulnerable to perceptual ambiguities and illusions. The CPD theory further predicts that impairing the feedback renders the flip tilt illusion visible in the central visual field. This paper reports a confirmation of the prediction. The feedback is disrupted by masking the visual inputs after a short viewing duration t. Furthermore, the FFVW algorithm is studied by a computational model of the perceptual data as a function of t. It reveals that the initial feedforward sweep of visual information explains the flip tilt illusion for t shorter than 20 ms, whereas the feedback mechanism dominates perception for longer t.

AI.tldr: This paper validates the Central-Peripheral Dichotomy (CPD) theory by demonstrating that the flip tilt illusion occurs in the peripheral field due to limited feedback mechanisms, and can be induced in the central field by masking visual inputs to disrupt the Feedforward-Feedback-Verify-reWeight (FFVW) algorithm.
AI.motivation: To investigate the mechanisms behind the flip tilt illusion using the Central-Peripheral Dichotomy (CPD) theory and the Feedforward-Feedback-Verify-reWeight (FFVW) algorithm.
AI.method: Experimental confirmation of the CPD theory through masking visual inputs after a short duration (t) and computational modeling of the FFVW algorithm to analyze perceptual data.
AI.result: Masking visual inputs disrupts the feedback mechanism, making the flip tilt illusion visible in the central field; computational modeling shows the initial feedforward sweep explains the illusion for t < 20 ms, while feedback dominates for longer durations.
AI.conclusion: The study confirms that the flip tilt illusion is a result of perceptual ambiguity in the periphery caused by limited feedback/re-weighting, and that the effect can be extended to the central field by disrupting feedback.

title: Analysis of Biomarkers from Visual Explorations in Individuals Suspected to Be in the Prodromal Phase of Parkinson's Disease
summary: Identifying prodromal Parkinson's Disease is a precondition for any future treatment that modifies the course of the disease, since such therapies would ideally act on the initial pathogenic events, early enough to delay the clinical onset of the disease rather than only slow its progression. In this work, a visual exploration model is retrained on an expanded corpus. Without any further training or threshold recalibration, it is then tested on an enriched cohort of patients with high risk of being in the prodromal phase of Parkinson's Disease, testing whether the learned signal follows a continuum of disease rather than only separating patients from controls. The resulting score distribution is analysed as an external evaluation of the hypothesis that the oculomotor signature targeted by the model is already partly present before clinical diagnosis. With every subject scored on data not used to train the model, the scores are ordered as controls < high-risk patients < Parkinson's Disease, with 42% of the high-risk patients exceeding the decision threshold. A SHAP decomposition of the scores into classifiers and gaze features shows that high scores in this cohort are driven mainly by reduced saccadic excursion, fewer fixations and longer fixations, the hypokinetic oculomotor profile that characterises Parkinson's Disease. The model score is also compared against the prodromal markers used for recruitment. The score is not correlated with hyposmia, constipation, depression or REM sleep behaviour disorder; these results, interpreted in the context of the selection induced by the recruitment criteria, are discussed as evidence that within the high-risk cohort the score is largely not explained by the available ancillary clinical variables. The results suggest that the visual biomarkers analysed are a complementary indicator to identify patients at risk of being in the prodromal stage.

AI.tldr: The study evaluates whether a visual exploration model trained on Parkinson's Disease (PD) patients can detect early (prodromal) signs of the disease in high-risk individuals via oculomotor signatures.
AI.motivation: To identify PD during the prodromal phase, allowing for disease-modifying therapies to act before clinical onset.
AI.method: A visual exploration model was retrained on an expanded corpus and tested on a high-risk cohort (without recalibration). The researchers analyzed score distributions and used SHAP decomposition to identify the specific gaze features driving the scores.
AI.result: The model demonstrated a disease continuum (Controls < High-Risk < PD). Notably, 42% of high-risk patients exceeded the clinical decision threshold. High scores were driven by hypokinetic ocular patterns: reduced saccadic excursion, fewer fixations, and longer fixations.
AI.conclusion: The oculomotor signature is present before clinical diagnosis and is not explained by common prodromal markers (hyposmia, constipation, etc.), suggesting visual biomarkers are a valuable, independent tool for early PD detection.

title: Intrinsic Goals for Autonomous Agents: Hierarchical Exploration Captures Future Volitional Action in Drosophila
comment: 27 pages, 5 figures
summary: Animals have a remarkable capacity for autonomy---driven by intrinsic motivation---without external sensory cues or extrinsic objectives, yet the computational mechanisms behind this ability largely remain a mystery. We combine whole-brain recordings in the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), which reveal neural representations of spontaneous exploratory decisions more than 10 seconds in advance, with a neuromechanical digital twin to test whether optimizing intrinsic goals yields realistically embodied artificial agents that quantitatively match fly behavior and internal representations of future volitional action during exploration. Our hierarchical policy selects from a discrete library of low-level motor primitives, consistent with ethological theories of behavioral syllables. We train agents without external reward using 20 intrinsic motivation algorithms spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency methods. The agents are evaluated in a virtual tethered-ball assay modeled on the fly experiment, comparing spontaneous locomotor statistics and internal representations and decoding future turn direction from kinematics and neural activity on the same timescales observed in flies. DIAYN, a hierarchical competency algorithm learning discrete policies that maximize behavioral entropy and the separability of induced sensory observations, achieves the strongest joint behavioral and neural prospective coding performance relative to flies. Its learned policies closely capture individual variability in fly exploration strategies, suggesting that this diversity serves to maximize state-space coverage at the population level. DIAYN's latent activity also closely captures the sum-difference rule for interhemispheric encoding of kinematics in biological flies. These results establish hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agents as a powerful framework for reverse-engineering animal autonomy.

AI.tldr: The study uses a 'neuromechanical digital twin' to reverse-engineer how fruit flies exhibit autonomous exploration driven by intrinsic motivation rather than external rewards.
AI.motivation: To understand the computational mechanisms behind animal autonomy and spontaneous decision-making.
AI.method: Researchers combined whole-brain recordings of *Drosophila* with a digital twin agent. They tested 20 intrinsic motivation algorithms (curiosity, entropy, competency) using a hierarchical policy of motor primitives within a virtual tethered-ball assay.
AI.result: The **DIAYN** (Diversity Is All You Need) algorithm—a hierarchical competency method—best matched biological fly behavior and neural representations. It successfully captured individual variability in exploration and the 'sum-difference rule' used in biological interhemispheric encoding.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agents provide a robust framework for reverse-engineering the neural and computational basis of animal autonomy.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Parkinson's Disease Classification from Resting-State Functional Connectivity
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures
summary: Altered resting-state functional connectivity (FC) is a candidate marker for the diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD). Publicly available PD datasets, however, are small and fragmented across sites, scanners and clinical criteria. Transfer learning mitigates data scarcity by reusing a model trained on larger cohorts, but represents their knowledge primarily through a single set of weights shared by all individuals. Motivated by precision neuroimaging, we propose a retrieval-augmented classification (RAC) framework that additionally places each target individual in the context of similar individuals from external cohorts. A graph convolutional autoencoder (GAE), trained on external PD and control cohorts, encodes these cohorts into a neuro-knowledge base. Each target individual is encoded using the pretrained GAE, and its nearest neighbors are retrieved from the external knowledge base. Their embeddings are combined with the target embedding using mean aggregation or attention for classification. A systematic comparison on the TaoWu cohort separated the contributions of encoder pretraining, retrieval, attention and partial fine-tuning. Pretraining improved mean classification accuracy from 60.5% to 66.0%. However, retrieval and attention did not consistently improve performance over the pretrained-only variants. Several retrieval-based configurations nevertheless showed modestly higher ROC-AUC than the randomly initialized baseline. Varying the number of retrieved neighbors and partially fine-tuning the encoder provided no consistent additional gains. Retrieval-neighborhood analysis further showed diagnostically mixed neighborhoods. These findings provide initial evidence that population-learned representations can be complemented by individual-specific retrieval in neuroimaging, although larger datasets are needed to determine when such contextual information improves classification.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a **Retrieval-Augmented Classification (RAC)** framework to address data scarcity in Parkinson's disease (PD) neuroimaging by combining transfer learning with a retrieval mechanism.
AI.motivation: Publicly available PD datasets are small and fragmented. While transfer learning helps, standard models use shared weights that may fail to capture individual-specific nuances (precision neuroimaging).
AI.method:
1. **Pretraining**: A Graph Convolutional Autoencoder (GAE) is trained on large external cohorts to create a 'neuro-knowledge base'.
2. **Retrieval**: For a target individual, the GAE encodes them and retrieves 'nearest neighbors' from the knowledge base.
3. **Aggregation**: Target and retrieved embeddings are combined via mean aggregation or attention mechanisms for final classification.
AI.result:
1. **Positive**: Pretraining the encoder significantly boosted accuracy (60.5% $\rightarrow$ 66.0%).
2. **Mixed**: Retrieval and attention mechanisms did **not** consistently improve performance over pretraining alone.
3. **Observation**: Retrieval-neighborhood analysis showed 'diagnostically mixed' results, suggesting that finding similar individuals is difficult in current datasets.
AI.conclusion: While population-level representations are highly beneficial, the effectiveness of individual-specific retrieval remains unproven and likely requires much larger datasets to demonstrate a consistent advantage.

title: The mathematical journey of spatial reciprocity
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures
summary: Over the past three decades, evolutionary game theory in structured populations has witnessed explosive progress. Counterintuitive cooperative phenomena discovered in simulations have stimulated the development of rigorous mathematical theories to describe the underlying dynamics. In this paper, we review these theoretical advancements, including pair approximation and coalescent theory, which offer analytical solutions to evolutionary games on networks. We summarize the key results obtained by these theories, while also discussing their limitations, such as high computational complexity and constrained flexibility when applied to complex models. We therefore suggest that mathematical approaches provide a complementary tool for understanding cooperation in structured populations alongside simulations.

AI.tldr: A review of mathematical theories (pair approximation and coalescent theory) used to analytically explain cooperative phenomena in evolutionary games on structured networks.
AI.motivation: To review and summarize the theoretical progress in evolutionary game theory within structured populations, addressing the gap between simulation-based discoveries and rigorous mathematical explanations.
AI.method: A comprehensive review of theoretical advancements in evolutionary game theory, specifically focusing on pair approximation and coalescent theory for analyzing games on networks.
AI.result: Summary of key analytical solutions for evolutionary games on networks and an identification of limitations such as high computational complexity and limited flexibility in complex models.
AI.conclusion: Mathematical approaches like pair approximation and coalescent theory are essential complementary tools to simulations for understanding cooperation in structured populations.

title: mdRNAcat: A Molecular Dynamics RNA Catalog of REST2 Conformational Ensembles
comment: 24 pages, 9 figures. Dataset and accompanying resources available on Hugging Face under the HelmholtzAI-FZJ organization
summary: Learning molecular models of RNA requires simulation data that capture conformational variability and provide consistent physical training signals. Here, we introduce mdRNAcat, a curated dataset of all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of 48 RNA systems selected to promote sequence diversity. Each system is simulated using replica-exchange with solute scaling (REST2), with 32 Hamiltonian states and production lengths of 200-300 ns per state. The dataset provides atomic coordinates, instantaneous forces, and forces reevaluated under the unscaled reference Hamiltonian, together with structural annotations and replica-exchange metadata. Coordinates and forces are available at 1 ps intervals for the reference state and 100 ps intervals across all states in a standardized HDF5 format. We characterize conformational sampling, exchange behavior, base pairing, and sugar-pucker distributions to document the properties of the simulated ensembles. mdRNAcat provides a reusable resource for developing and evaluating data-driven RNA models, including coarse-grained force fields.

AI.tldr: A new, diverse, and physically rich MD simulation dataset (mdRNAcat) specifically built to train and evaluate data-driven RNA models.
AI.motivation: Current RNA modeling lacks sufficient simulation data that captures both **conformational variability** and **consistent physical training signals** (forces) necessary for accurate machine learning training.
AI.method: The researchers utilized **Replica-Exchange with Solute Scaling (REST2)** to simulate 48 diverse RNA systems. They employed 32 Hamiltonian states with production runs of 200–300 ns per state, ensuring enhanced conformational sampling.
